newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam to return Agent Orange papers to scientist.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam to return Agent Orange papers to scientist.

text.p: Vietnam's committee for research into the effect of Agent Orange, the defoliant sprayed by U.S. forces during the Vietnam War, has agreed to return documents seized from an American scientist at Hanoi airport two years ago.
An official at the 10-80 Committee said on Monday that some, but not all, of the papers seized by customs would be sent back to Dr Arnold Schecter of the State University of New York.

The offer to return the documents and resume collaboration on research into the effects of dioxin, a harmful chemical in Agent Orange, came just days before a conference in Hanoi to examine possible lessons from the conflict, which ended in 1975.
The United States' Vietnam War Defence Secretary, Robert Macnamara, and about 50 American researchers and historians will attend the June 20-23 meeting with government ministers and academics.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright is due to visit Hanoi three days after that to discuss a range of issues, including efforts to account for U.S. personnel missing from the war and human rights.

The 10-80 official said that Committee Chairman Professor Hoang Dinh Cau wrote to Schecter last week, offering to give back the documents confiscated along with blood and food specimens after a 10-day scientific mission sponsored by the government.
Agent Orange was widely used in the Vietnam War to defoliate jungle areas used by Viet Cong and North Vietnamese troops.
U.S. and South Vietnamese aircraft sprayed about 12 million gallons (45.6 million litres) of Agent Orange over about 10 percent of what was then South Vietnam, mostly during the 1960s.
Schecter published research in 1995 which showed that people in what used to be South Vietnam had levels of dioxin that were up to 50 times higher than people in the north.
Many U.S. veterans exposed to the chemical blamed it for health problems and for birth defects suffered by their children.

Controversy over the effect of the herbicide raged in the United States for more than a decade and finally ended in 1993 when Congress authorised benefits for those with seven specific ailments linked to Agent Orange exposure.
In March last year, a panel of scientists reported to Congress that new studies had confirmed links between Agent Orange exposure during the war and cancers and other health problems.

The government-run Vietnam Investment Review on Monday ran a front-page article quoting the United States' new ambassador to Vietnam, Pete Peterson, as saying that it would take a long time to clarify the exact consequences of the defoliant.
Peterson, a fighter pilot and prisoner of war during the conflict, was quoted as saying that global scientific research was needed for a conclusion.
The journal described his comments as "discouraging" and ran a long article highlighting the ailments of Vietnamese war veterans exposed to Agent Orange and the deformities of their children.
The official Vietnam News Agency (VNA) on Sunday catalogued the cost of the war, saying three million Vietnamese had been killed, 4.4 million wounded and two million affected by toxic chemicals.
VNA gave no explanation for the timing of its report.
